written: 1863-06-28 (letter, Carlisle, Pa.); transcription posted by UNC Libraries 2013-06-28
rights_basis: Unpublished 1863 manuscript by L. L. Polk (1837-1892 per UNC finding aid), so the author's life+70 term ended before 1963 and the letter is public domain in the US on the author-death basis, not an imprint-year basis. UNC finding aid for L.L. Polk Papers #3708 (fetched via the 301 chain to finding-aids.lib.unc.edu/catalog/03708): 'No usage restrictions', copyright 'retained by the authors ... or their descendants'. The blog page itself carries no license; it sends X-Robots-Tag: noarchive (an indexing hint, not a license). UNC owns the transcription/blog layer, so counsel should confirm before bulk reuse.
evidence: Fetched blogs.lib.unc.edu entry URL -> 302 -> https://web.lib.unc.edu/civilwar/index.php/2013/06/28/28-june-1863/ (200, 43,063 B; blogs.lib robots.txt 200 disallows only /wp-admin/; web.lib robots.txt 404). Page = UNC 'Civil War Day by Day', posted by Biff Hollingsworth: 'Letter, 28 June 1863, from Second Lieutenant Leonidas L. Polk to his wife', 'Leonidas La Fayette Polk (1837-1892) of Anson County, N.C. ... 26th and 43rd North Carolina', from folder 2b of the L.L. Polk Papers #3708, SHC, Wilson Library, followed by 'Item Transcription'. I downloaded the page's three manuscript scans (web.lib.unc.edu/civilwar/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/186306280001/2/3 jpgs) and read sheets 1-2: the heading 'Carlisle Pa. June 28th 1863', 'My own dear Wife', the 74-miles-in-2.5-days sentence and the postscript about Pettigrew, cattle and horses all match the transcription. Description claims checked: (a) Confederate soldier's letter from Pennsylvania: dateline Carlisle, signed Leonidas, writer says Rhodes Division, Daniels Brigade; (b) transcribed by UNC Libraries: yes. UNC finding aid (fetched) says Polk was 2nd Lt. of the 43rd NC Infantry, Company I, so the entry's '43rd' is independently confirmed. OR I/27/2 (Rodes's report, cached historian-src/raw/or27/normalized-2.txt ~l.47360) lists Daniel's brigade as 32nd, 43rd, 45th, 53rd NC and 2nd NC Bn, and says the brigades of Daniel, Iverson and Ramseur occupied the US barracks at Carlisle on 27 June; the letter says 'we are now occupying the barracks'.
extraction_notes: One WordPress post = one letter. Body text is a continuous transcription (paragraphs plus two postscript blocks); sheet breaks are not marked, but the three sheets are shown as images. Segment by paragraph (about 5 passages). Cite as L. L. Polk to his wife, 28 June 1863, L.L. Polk Papers #3708, SHC, UNC, via UNC Libraries. Before any verbatim quote is shipped, re-check it against the scans: on sheet 2 the manuscript appears to read 'Tell Father to write home', but the UNC transcription reads 'write to me' (my reading; moderate-to-high confidence).
issues: Title 'Leonidas Polk letter' collides with Confederate Lt. Gen. Leonidas Polk (the bishop-general, 1806-1864, in Tennessee in June 1863). Author is Leonidas L. (La Fayette) Polk, 2nd Lt., 43rd N.C. Retitle to 'Leonidas L. Polk letter to his wife, 28 June 1863'. The UNC tag 'Leonidas Polk' perpetuates the ambiguity.
Written 28 June 1863, before the fighting: campaign context only, no Gettysburg action described.
Host redirects blogs.lib.unc.edu -> web.lib.unc.edu; use the web.lib.unc.edu URL.
UNC transcription is not guaranteed verbatim (suspected 'write home' vs 'write to me' on sheet 2).
No license on the page; X-Robots-Tag: noarchive; repository finding aid says no usage restrictions: record both when host terms are reviewed.

written: 1863-06-28 (letter; PDF scan posted by House Divided 2018-06-12)
rights_basis: Unpublished 1863 letter; author William Jackson Underwood (1840-1864 per AHC finding aid), so the life+70 term expired by 1934 and it is public domain in the US on the author-death basis. But the holding repository (Atlanta History Center, Kenan Research Center, MSS 213) states 'Unpublished manuscripts are protected by copyright. All requests to publish, quote, or reproduce must be submitted through the Kenan Research Center.' House Divided hosts the PDF with no rights statement. So: needs review, and the safe course is a link-out unless the AHC permits quoting.
evidence: URL http://housedivided.dickinson.edu/.../Underwood-June-28-1-3.pdf -> 301 to https -> 200 application/pdf, 8,204,661 B, Last-Modified 12 Jun 2018 (host robots.txt 404). PDF metadata: title 'Underwood June 28', author 'Cooper Wingert' (House Divided staff), created with Preview. 3 pages, no text layer (0 characters per page), rendered and read visually: p1 'Camp in the Park of Dickinson College / Carlisle Penn. / June 28th 1863 / Messrs ... & M.L. Underwood / My Dear Little Brothers'; p2 'We are now 18 miles of Harrisburg', three letters written since the march began at Culpeper C.H., Williamsport Md. and Greencastle Pa., and an archive stamp '77-535-09B'; p3 (smaller landscape sheet) signs off 'your Brother W.J. Underwood'. Independent confirmation of the entry's unshown claims: the House Divided source post (fetched) credits the letter to the Atlanta History Center, and I fetched AHC finding aid MSS 213 'Underwood, Key families papers' (via ahc.galileo.usg.edu 302 -> aspace-atlantahistorycenter.galileo.usg.edu/repositories/2/resources/408; 200): 'William Jackson Underwood (Jacky) served in the 4th Regiment, Georgia Volunteers, Company F', brothers James Knox Polk and Marion LaFayette (matching the addressees M.L. and J.K.P.), acquisition number 1977.535 (matches the scan stamp), letters including 'his participation in the battle at Gettysburg'. OR I/27/2 (Rodes's report, cached normalized-2.txt l.47755) says Doles's brigade bivouacked on the campus of Dickinson College at Carlisle, and Doles's brigade is the 4th, 12th, 21st and 44th Georgia (l.47369): consistent with a 4th Georgia soldier in 'the Park of Dickinson College'.
extraction_notes: Image-only PDF, handwritten manuscript (3 raster pages, handwriting, no OCR). No machine-readable text exists, so 'free full text' is not true here. Any text would be our own transcription of a handwritten letter, and the AHC's quoting restriction applies. Page 3 is a separate smaller sheet that continues mid-sentence from p2 (page order assumed from the file). Link-out only until the AHC replies or counsel clears it.
issues: No free full text: image-only scan, handwriting.

'4th Georgia' and 'Atlanta History Center' are not on the PDF itself: confirmed only via the House Divided post and AHC MSS 213 (accession 1977.535 matches the stamp).
Title page of letter lacks any regiment; identification of W. J. Underwood as the 4th Georgia soldier rests on the AHC finding aid.
Campaign-period (Carlisle, 28 June); no battle account.

written: 1863-07-10 (letter from Staunton, Va., six days after the writer left Gettysburg)
rights_basis: CONTENTdm item record (dmGetItemInfo civilwar/2007, fetched) states: 'Public Domain. For further information please contact University of South Carolina, Irvin Department of Rare Books and Special Collections and/or South Caroliniana Library'. Unpublished 1863 manuscript; no adult of 1863 can plausibly have lived past 1955, so the life+70 term has expired. Repository metadata plus the date on the manuscript support A1 for the content; our own transcription would be needed to quote it.
evidence: http://digital.tcl.sc.edu/cdm/ref/collection/civilwar/id/2007 -> 301 -> 301 -> https://digital.tcl.sc.edu/digital/collection/civilwar/id/2007 (200, 55 KB, a JavaScript viewer shell; robots.txt 200, Crawl-Delay 1, disallows only /digital/collection/civilwar/search/). Item metadata (https://digital.tcl.sc.edu/digital/bl/dmwebservices/index.php?q=dmGetItemInfo/civilwar/2007/json): title 'Letter, 10 July 1863, from Wesley Watson, Staunton, Va., to his brother', creator 'Watson, Wesley', date 1863-07-10, source 'Watson Family Papers; Accession no. 13960', subjects '6th Alabama Infantry, Company G' and 'Gettysburg, Battle of', cdmhasocr 0 (no text layer). Compound object = 3 page images (ptr 2004, 2005 a two-page spread, 2006), fetched via IIIF and read: p1 'Staunton Va July 10th 1863 / My Dear Brother', calls it the greatest of modern battles, estimates 20,000 Confederate losses, reports enemy losses of 60,000 and 40,000 prisoners (rumor), 'on Saturday the day I left Gettysburg'; spread says he came to Staunton with 'Col Lightfoot and Major Culver of my regiment' wounded, that Yankee officers surrendered to him and he took a sword, that Ewell's corps went to Carlisle and rejoined Longstreet and Hill; and 'a long conversation with Dr. Johnson the morning I left' Carlisle ('principles are as bad as Wm H Seward's ... an unmitigated abolitionist and a bitter enemy to the south'); p3 is signed 'Wesley' and mentions a night attack on South Mountain that captured about 200 wagons. OR I/27/2 casualty list (cached normalized-2.txt l.48760) confirms 'Col. J. N. Lightfoot, 6th Alabama' and 'Maj. J. F. Culver, 6th Alabama' wounded 1 July.
extraction_notes: CONTENTdm compound object, 3 JP2 images served through IIIF (https://digital.tcl.sc.edu/digital/iiif/civilwar/<ptr>/full/1400,/0/default.jpg); no transcript or OCR. A human must transcribe it (3 pages, legible copperplate hand) and a second person must check it against the scans before any passage enters the corpus; until then use as a link-out. Segment by paragraph/page; cite as Wesley Watson to his brother, 10 July 1863, Watson Family Papers, South Caroliniana Library, via USC Digital Collections.
issues: Entry gives no date; the letter is 10 July 1863 and is mainly a Gettysburg-participant account (1 July fighting, capturing officers, the wagon-train retreat), richer than the description says.

'Elihu Wesley Watson' and 'private' come from the House Divided post only: the CONTENTdm record says 'Watson, Wesley', the letter is signed 'Wesley', and the letter never states his rank (he says he captured Union officers and sword). Treat the name and rank as unverified.
'Herman Johnson' is not named in the letter: it says 'Dr. Johnson' in Carlisle (the identification as Dickinson president Herman Johnson is the House Divided post's inference, plausible).
No free full text: image-only.
Casualty and prisoner numbers are the writer's rumors (60,000 enemy loss, 40,000 prisoners) and are wrong as history; flag in any card.
http link: use https.

written: daily entries 1863-06-24 to 1863-07-08; transcription PDF made 2018-08-09
rights_basis: Anonymous, unpublished 1863 diary; under 17 U.S.C. 302(c) a work made for no named author lasts 120 years from creation, which ended in 1983, so the diary is public domain. The PDF is a Word-made transcription by Frank Kline (per the House Divided post) of a manuscript held by the Cumberland County Historical Society (per the same post); neither the PDF nor the post gives a rights statement, and the Dickinson host asserts site copyright. Needs review of transcriber/CCHS terms.
evidence: http://housedivided.dickinson.edu/.../1863-Young-Girls-Pocket-Diary-CCHS.pdf -> 301 -> 200 application/pdf, 32,288 B, Last-Modified 9 Aug 2018; 2 pages, text layer (PyMuPDF 4,130 chars). PDF title 'Microsoft Word - 1863 Young Girl's Pocket Diary CCHS.docx', no author field. 15 dated entries, 'Wednesday, June 24, 1863' to 'Wednesday, July 8, 1863'. Description check: the 'Monday, June 29, 1863' entry reads 'The Rebels are going in every house and stealing all they can' (verbatim in the PDF), matching the entry's paraphrase and the House Divided post's quote. Second claim: the Saturday 27 June entry says the Rebels entered town at ten o'clock with 'General Jenkins- Brigade of Calvary' (Ewell's corps), and 1 July says about seven in the evening the Rebels shelled the town and the garrison burned; OR I/27/2 (cached normalized-2.txt ll.16470, 20213-20225) says Ewell's corps occupied Carlisle on the 27th and on 1 July Stuart's cavalry shelled it and burned the barracks. The 1 July 'about 10,000 of our troops ... three batteries' is the diarist's figure; OR l.16506 gives Gen. W. F. Smith's force as about 3,000. Provenance and 'transcribed by Frank Kline' / 'CCHS' come from the House Divided post (fetched 2018-06-11 'Beyond Gettysburg: Primary Sources for the Gettysburg Campaign' by Cooper Wingert), not from the PDF text.
extraction_notes: Clean text PDF, 2 pages, plain chronological entries (15 dated entries). Segment one passage per dated entry. Cite as Anonymous Carlisle diarist, pocket diary 1863, Cumberland County Historical Society, transcribed by Frank Kline, via Dickinson College House Divided Project. The transcription has bracketed text like '[4]' and misspellings ('Getesburg', 'bruned') that must be kept verbatim. Not checkable against the manuscript (no scan online).
issues: Anonymous: no author, repository or transcriber named in the PDF; 'CCHS' and 'Frank Kline' come from the PDF filename and the House Divided post only.
'Young girl' is a catalog/post label; the text does not state age or sex.
Transcription only, unchecked against a scan.
Battle content is only second-hand rumor (July 5: 'we captured 118 cannon 25,000 prisoners'); relevance is the Carlisle occupation, shelling and aftermath.
Entry title says June-July 1863; the entries run 24 June to 8 July.
Troop figure (10,000) conflicts with OR (about 3,000): diarist's estimate.
http link: use https.

rights_basis: Title page: Lieutenant General Jubal Anderson Early, C.S.A.: Autobiographical Sketch and Narrative of the War Between the States, with notes by R. H. Early, J. B. Lippincott Company, Philadelphia and London, 1912; copyright notice 1912 Lippincott. US imprint before 1931. Internet Archive/Cornell scan (cu31924030913630): 'There are no known copyright restrictions in the United States on the use of the text.' Use only the 1912 imprint: the IA search also lists copyrighted reprints (Indiana University Press 1960, Broadfoot 1989, Nautical & Aviation 1989), which must be excluded from the allow-list.
evidence: The exact entry URL has dq= and pg= parameters, which books.google.com/robots.txt disallows (/books?*dq=, /books?*pg=), so I did not fetch it. I fetched the bare https://books.google.com/books?id=0xtCAAAAIAAJ (200): 'Lieutenant General Jubal Anderson Early, C.S.A.: Autobiographical Sketch and ...', Jubal Anderson Early, editor Ruth Hairston Early, J.B. Lippincott 1912, 496 pages, original from University of California, 'Full view'. I then fetched the Cornell copy from archive.org (metadata API 200; item page 200; _djvu.txt 1.19 MB; _page_numbers.json): leaf 298 = printed p.257. The OCR shows p.257 is Early at Gettysburg on 26 June (the 26th Pennsylvania Militia fled), p.258 has him at Mummasburg; York begins p.259; p.260 describes Gordon at Wrightsville finding the bridge already burning and the town fire; p.261 the York levy of $28,600 and 1,200-1,500 pairs of shoes; p.262 footnote reproduces Early's 'To the Citizens of York' address. The memoir's York passage is an expansion of his official report of 22 Aug 1863 (OR I/27/2 No. 470, cached normalized-2.txt l.40891, bridge passage l.41380), so it is not independent evidence. Description claims verified: (a) division's occupation of York: pp.259-262; (b) burning of the Wrightsville bridge: p.260 ('inflammable materials having previously been prepared').
extraction_notes: Use the IA OCR text (cu31924030913630_djvu.txt, 1,194,554 B, no form-feed page breaks; printed page numbers appear as lone numerals before each running head; use _page_numbers.json to map leaves to printed pages and _djvu.xml for page boxes). The running-head section 'AT YORK AND WRIGHTSVILLE' starts at p.253; the York and Wrightsville passage is pp.258-262 (leaves 299-303). OCR is good with some errors ('Eodes', 'Greneral', 'burniag', 'G-ordon'). Footnotes (p.262 York address) are separate primary text in the same imprint. Cite 'Early, Autobiographical Sketch and Narrative (Lippincott, 1912), p. 260, via Internet Archive'.
issues: Exact Google Books URL (dq=, pg=PA257) disallowed by robots.txt and not fetched; only the bare id page was checked.
Page anchor is off by two pages: p.257 is Early's 26 June occupation of Gettysburg; York begins p.259 and the bridge burning is on p.260. Section 'At York and Wrightsville' starts p.253.

Retrospective and self-justifying memoir written decades later; tag as retrospective with a self-justifying/Lost Cause flag. His statement that the militia burned the bridge is his own account, and he also describes enemy 'barbarous policy'.
Not independent of his 1863 official report (OR I/27/2 No. 470).
Title 'memoir pages' is vague; the 1866/67 'A Memoir of the Last Year of the War for Independence' is a different work covering only 1864-65.
Figures differ slightly from entry 593's newspaper account ($28,600 vs $28,000).

written: newspaper account published July-August 1863 in the Baltimore Gazette (exact date not given); reprinted in the Raleigh Daily Progress on 14 Aug 1863 (per the blog, unverified); blog post 2015-10-22, modified 2020-10-08
rights_basis: The 1863 newspaper text is public domain, but the only copy reached is the blogger's transcription with his own bracketed editorial insertions on a page marked '(c) 2026 York Daily Record/Sunday News'. The original newspaper page (Baltimore Gazette or Raleigh Daily Progress) was not located, so there is no verified A1 source. Link-out only; if the original page image is found on Chronicling America or similar, it could be re-sourced as A1.
evidence: http URL -> 301 -> https://www.yorkblog.com/... -> 302 -> https://yorkblog.com/cannonball/eyewitness-account-of-the-confederate-occupation-of-york-pa/ (200, 61 KB, yorkblog.com robots.txt 200 'Disallow:' empty). Page title 'New eyewitness account of the Confederate occupation of York, Pa. - Cannonball', by Scott Mingus, 22 Oct 2015 (Yoast published 2015-10-23T02:13Z, modified 2020-10-08). Blog states the Daily Progress of Raleigh on Friday 14 Aug 1863 repeated a story from the Baltimore Gazette, 'an account written by an eyewitness here in York'. The excerpt describes Gordon's brigade entering York on Sunday 28 June at 10 AM with a band playing Dixie, Early's headquarters at the court house, a demand for '$100,00' (sic) and rations, and a result of $28,000 and 30,000 rations. Cross-checks against entry 592 (Early 1912, pp.259-262): Gordon entered York on the 28th, Early levied $100,000, shoes, hats, socks and rations, and received $28,600 and 1,200-1,500 pairs of shoes. Second claim: the excerpt's Early 'inspected the railroad properties' and burned only a few old cars; Early's memoir says he spared the car factories and depots and burned only some cars. I tried two Chronicling America (loc.gov, Crawl-Delay 5) full-text searches and did not find the Daily Progress page.
extraction_notes: HTML page: blogger introduction, then about nine paragraphs of quoted newspaper text interrupted by the blogger's square-bracket editor's notes, then tags. If it were ever used the quoted block would have to be stripped of the bracketed notes and the typo '$100,00' flagged. Better to re-source the original 1863 text from a newspaper page image (citation 'title, date, page').
issues: Author unidentified; the Baltimore Gazette original and its date are not given; the item is a reprint of a reprint with a blogger's transcription, unchecked against a page image.
Daily Progress date (14 Aug 1863) is the blog's statement; not verified.
Host copyright (York Daily Record); quotable 1863 text must be re-sourced from the original paper.
Blogger's bracketed editorial notes are inside the quoted text.
Transcription slip: '$100,00' for $100,000.
Entry title omits the newspaper name and date; 'civilian' status of the writer is inferred from 'our citizens' phrasing.
URL as listed redirects (http to https, date path removed); use the canonical URL.

rights_basis: Title page: History of the Twenty-second Regiment of the National Guard of the State of New York from its Organization to 1895, by General George W. Wingate, Edwin W. Dayton, New York, 'Copyright, 1896'. Cornell/Internet Archive scan cu31924030725166: 'There are no known copyright restrictions in the United States on the use of the text.' US imprint before 1931. Google Books lists later 2015 and 2018 reprints with no preview, which must not be used.
evidence: The exact URL (dq=, pg=PA193) is disallowed for bots by books.google.com/robots.txt, so I did not fetch it. I fetched the bare https://books.google.com/books?id=CJQQAAAAYAAJ (200): 'History of the Twenty-second Regiment of the National Guard of the State of New York: From Its Organization to 1895', George Wood Wingate, E. W. Dayton, 1896, 762 pages, original from Harvard, 'Full view'. I fetched the Cornell copy at archive.org (metadata 200, 830 images; _djvu.txt 1.37 MB; _page_numbers.json: leaf 232 = printed p.193). The contents list Chapter XVIII 'Oyster Point' (p.192) and the text reads: at about 10 on the morning of 30 June Brig. Gen. Ewen ordered the 22nd and 37th N.Y.N.G. to prepare for a four-hour march; p.193 describes the march, Jenkins's brigade of Stuart's cavalry and the countermarch; p.194 the volley from the wood and the barn, Lt. Rufus King sending Companies A and C into the wood; p.195 Landis's battery arrives at a gallop; the fight runs pp.194-197 and the chapter to p.199. Wingate cites Gen. Smith's report calling it Sporting Hill (Oyster Point) at p.226. Description claims verified: (a) participant author: the roster lists George W. Wingate in the regiment, and the narrative says a detachment of black laborers at the fortifications 'were put under the command of the writer' in June 1863; he also wrote to Col. T. S. Garnett for the Confederate side; (b) Sporting Hill covered: pp.192-199, with the action itself on pp.194-197.
extraction_notes: Use IA OCR (cu31924030725166_djvu.txt, no page-break characters; running heads carry the printed page numbers; _page_numbers.json maps leaves to printed pages, e.g. leaf 232 = p.193, leaf 233 = p.194). Chapter XVIII pp.192-199; the OCR is good with a few errors. The narrative is third-person, built partly from the Official Records and quoted participant accounts (George E. Pearce's Tribune letter at p.195, a footnote), so the quotes inside it are other people's words; attribute them separately. Cite 'Wingate, History of the Twenty-second Regiment (Dayton, 1896), p. 194, via Internet Archive'.
issues: Exact Google Books URL (dq=, pg=PA193) disallowed by robots.txt and not fetched; only the bare id page and the IA copy were verified.
Page anchor: PA193 is the march and countermarch just before contact; the engagement starts p.194 and the chapter p.192.

Retrospective (1896) compilation partly reconstructed from the OR and other people's accounts: a hybrid of participant recollection and secondary history. For first-hand 1863 wording, prefer the contemporaneous Tribune account Wingate quotes.
Chapter title says 'Oyster Point' while the entry and OR call it Sporting Hill: search terms need both names.
Google Books scan is labelled 'Volume 22, Part 4' (an odd record label); printed pages agree with the IA copy.
Entry title gives '22nd New York State National Guard'; the work's title is 'Twenty-second Regiment of the National Guard of the State of New York'.

written: written 1865 from notes taken at the time; published 1899
rights_basis: Title page: History of the Ninth Virginia Cavalry in the War between the States, by the late Brig. General R. L. T. Beale, B. F. Johnson Publishing Company, Richmond, 1899. Internet Archive metadata (NYPL scan, fetched): date 1899, possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT. US imprint before 1931.
evidence: https://archive.org/stream/historyofninthvi00beal#page/84/mode/2up -> 301 to https://archive.org/details/historyofninthvi00beal?view=theater (200). Metadata API: 'History of the Ninth Virginia cavalry, in the war between the states', Beale, R. L. T. (Richard Lee Tuberville), 1819-1893, Richmond, B. F. Johnson, 1899, imagecount 208, description 'Written in 1865; found among the author's papers after his death'. I read the full _djvu.txt (411,982 B) and _page_numbers.json (leaf 96 = printed p.84, leaf 91 = p.83; plates sit between). Introductory note: written in 1865, found after Beale died on 17 April 1893, 'carefully copied' and arranged into chapters by 'G. W. B.', with a roster added. Chapter VIII (p.76 on) follows Stuart's ride through Rockville, Westminster, Hanover (30 June) and Carlisle; p.84 reads: a demand to surrender the place was declined, 'our cannons opened', the US barracks blazed, and the author, in charge of the wagon train, led it off to Papertown; he recalls hunting those grounds 'when a student at Dickinson College'; then Gettysburg (about 3 PM on the next day, Colonel J. Lucius Davis commanding the brigade) and Chapter IX the retreat. OR I/27/2 organization list (cached normalized-2.txt l.24027): 'W. H. F. Lee's Brigade, Col. J. R. Chambliss ... 9th Virginia, Col. R. L. T. Beale; 10th Virginia, Col. J. Lucius Davis'. Description claims verified: (a) by the 9th Virginia Cavalry's colonel: internal evidence shows the narrator ('the author') is the colonel (he is sick on reaching Virginia, takes a ten-day leave, and is struck in the leg on 13 September, the chapter heading's 'Colonel Beale Wounded'); (b) covers Stuart's ride and the July 1 shelling of Carlisle (the book gives no date for the shelling; it follows from the sequence after Hanover on 30 June).
extraction_notes: Internet Archive scan (NYPL): _djvu.txt 412 KB, no page-break characters; printed pages appear as running heads such as 'History of the Ninth Virginia Cavalry. 84' with OCR variants ('8 /J.', '8j') and bracketed numbers at chapter starts ('[77]'). _page_numbers.json gives leaf-to-page mapping (leaf 96 = p.84; plates at leaves 92-95 shift numbering). OCR has typical noise ('Mr- ginia', 'AVary'). Chapter VIII is pp.76-89 and chapter IX pp.90-97 (retreat). Narrator refers to himself as 'the author', 'the writer', 'the Colonel' and 'Lieutenant Beale', so quote cards should say Beale, History of the Ninth Virginia Cavalry (Richmond, 1899), p. 84, via Internet Archive. Chapter headings and roster are the 1899 editor's.
issues: Retrospective: written 1865 from notes (about two years later) and published 1899; reflects hindsight.
Editor G. W. B. (his son) 'carefully copied' the manuscript and added chapter headings and the roster: chapter titles are not the author's.

The author narrates in the third person ('the author', 'the writer', 'the Colonel', 'Lieutenant Beale'), so attribution to Beale rests on the title page, the introductory note and internal evidence (leave and wound in September 1863).
'Dickinson Class of 1838' is not in the book (it says only 'a student at Dickinson College'); it comes from the House Divided post.
The book does not date the shelling; July 1 is inferred from the sequence.
archive.org/stream/ URL redirects to the details page; the #page/84 fragment maps to printed p.84 via the page map.
OCR is noisy in places (page-number confidence low near plates, leaves 92-95).

written: 1863-07-13 (letter from 4 miles NW of Williamsport, MD, to the author's mother); printed 1883 in Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 11 (Jan-Dec 1883), no. 7 (July), pp. 320-327
rights_basis: Public domain by publication date, confirmed from the scans. The IA scan of vol. 11 has the title page 'JANUARY TO DECEMBER, 1883. RICHMOND, VA.: Rev. J. William Jones, D. D., Secretary Southern Historical Society'. A second scan, the original July issue, has the header 'Richmond, Va., July, 1883. No. 7.' Matter first published in 1883 is U.S. public domain. The IA vol. 11 item is a 1977 Kraus facsimile reprint (title page 'KRAUS REPRINT CO. Millwood, New York 1977'). A photographic reprint adds no new text rights, but the original-issue scan is the cleaner citation base. The gdg.org page carries no license or copyright notice: the host root, the /research/SHSP/ index and the page itself were checked, and the only 'permission' text is a photo credit on the home page. Its text is not a faithful copy of the print, so it should not be the quote source. The author's death date was not checked, so U.S. public-domain-by-date is the basis used and non-U.S. life-plus-years terms were not examined.

Its title page reads 'JANUARY TO DECEMBER, 1883' with the Kraus 1977 imprint, and its IA 'date' field says 1876 (series start, not the imprint). The contents line reads 'Gettysburg Campaign - A Soldier's Letter, by George W. Beale . 320'. The letter runs from the heading 'A Soldier's Account of the Gettysburg Campaign. Letter from George W. Beale (son of General R. L. T. Beale)' on p. 320 to 'G. W. Beale.' on p. 327. IA page_numbers.json puts printed p. 320 at leaf 330 and p. 327 at leaf 337. A second, separate scan, sim_southern-historical-society-papers_1883-07_11_7 (the original July 1883 issue from microfilm), contains the same letter on pp. 320-327 (leaves 31-38). THREE-WAY WORD DIFF (gdg.org vs both scans, normalised): about 3,405 words on gdg vs 3,434 and 3,431 in the scans. Where both scans agree and gdg differs there are about 20 differences: gdg omits 'through', 'to', 'had' (twice), 'though', 'and', 'a' and a 'that'; reads 'withing' for 'within', 'until' for 'till', 'up' for 'us' ('found up upon the mountain'), 'be' for 'he', 'in' for 'at' ('fight in Hagerstown'), 'effected' for 'effects', 'Devine' for 'Divine', 'endeavored' for 'endeavoured', 'Your son' for print 'You son'; and doubles 'many of the'. It also silently drops the print's quotation marks around 'lady's man'. So it is a clean-ish transcription but not verbatim. DESCRIPTION CHECK (two concrete claims). (1) 'Confederate cavalryman's account of Stuart's movements': the letter says 'our brigade, with General F. Lee's and Hampton's, started from Lovdon' and 'General Stuart headed the expedition', then walks Salem (Thursday, June [25]), Thoroughfare Gap, Fairfax C.H., the Potomac ford, Rockville, Westminster, Hanover, Carlisle ('General Stuart sent an order for its surrender, which was refused'), the Gettysburg arrival and East Cavalry Field, and Hagerstown. (2) 'Transcribed from SHSP': confirmed by the scan text above, with the deviations listed. INDEPENDENT FACT CROSS-CHECKS. (a) OR vol. 27 pt. 2, Stuart's report (corpus id or27-2:0565, read-only cache historian-src/raw/or27/passages.jsonl) says at Rockville 'More than one hundred and twenty-five best United States model wagons' were taken, with about 400 prisoners. Beale writes 'nearly two hundred wagons' and 'about 12,000 ... mules', so he exaggerates. The surrender demand at Carlisle, refused and then shelling, matches. Stuart names 'Lieut. Col. W. H. Payne, Fourth Virginia Cavalry' captured at Hanover, which matches Beale's 'Colonel Payne'. Stuart says the column moved out 'At 1 o'clock at night' against Beale's '3 o'clock A. M.'. Stuart's 'My advance reached Gettysburg July 2' is consistent with the letter. (b) R. L. T. Beale, History of the Ninth Virginia Cavalry (1899, archive.org historyofninthvi00beal): the roster lists 'Beale, George W ... First Lieutenant. Twice wounded', and the narrative says 'G. W. Beale was elected lieutenant in Company C'. The same book narrates 'Lieutenant Beale and Sergeant Richard Washington were leading' the charge on the guns near Hagerstown, with Washington found dead, and 'Lieutenant Beale was ordered to see that the remains ... were safely conveyed across the Potomac', matching the letter's Washington passage. (c) SHSP vol. 11 itself says R. L. T. Beale 'carried into the Ninth Virginia Cavalry his four sons'. This confirms the entry's '9th Virginia Cavalry' label, which the letter never states outright; the letter says 'the Thirteenth and Ninth Virginia ... were ordered to charge' at Hanover and 'This regiment and the Thirteenth' on 3 July. No other entry in entries.json shares this URL key. Entry 596 is the father's 1899 regimental history, a different work.
extraction_notes:
Take the text from the scan, not from gdg.org. Preferred source is the 1883 issue (replacement_url), leaves 31-38 = printed pp. 320-327. The Kraus reprint item southernhistoric0011sout (leaves 330-337) is the cross-check. Use it for the OCR base, which is ABBYY and generally better, and proof every passage against the page images, since both OCR layers have errors. Kraus OCR has 'io o'clock' for 10, 'wdthout', and 'terible'. The tesseract OCR of the 1883 issue loses spaces around dashes ('tiredexhausted', 'himone'), has 'meee' for 'melee' and '0'clock', and misreads 'Southern Historicel'. Strip the running heads ('Southern Historical Society Papers.' and 'The Gettysburg Campaign.') and the neighbouring items on p. 320 (anecdote tail) and p. 327 (start of Scheibert's notice). Re-join end-of-line hyphenations. Keep the print's own blanks, 'June - -' and 'Poor Eddie - -', and its typos ('You son', 'terible'), because they are verbatim. Segmentation: one metadata block (dateline, salutation, signature), then about 23 paragraphs, each cited as SHSP 11 (1883), p. N. Page-level citations are only possible from the scan. The gdg.org HTML has about 24

tags and no page breaks. Natural sub-segments are the ride (pp. 320-323), the Carlisle shelling (p. 323), Gettysburg 2-3 July (pp. 324-325), Hagerstown and Washington's death (pp. 325-326), and the closing paragraphs on the army and Pennsylvania depredations (p. 327). The letter has several clock times for the Historian's time claims: 3 A.M. at Salem, about 12 M. at the pickets, 'about dark', 'half-past 10 o'clock' and 'about 12 o'clock' on the cavalry fight. The days are relative ('next morning') and the date is left blank ('June - -'), so day assignment is by inference. East Cavalry Field is 3 July and Stuart's arrival is 2 July, matching Stuart's OR report. The text contains period racial terms in the narrative ('contrabands', 'runaway negroes', 'free negroes') and should be presented as period language.
issues: The listed URL is a volunteer transcription (Gettysburg Discussion Group, unchanged since 2010) with about 20 word-level deviations from the 1883 print: omitted words, 'withing', 'Devine', 'up' for 'us', 'be' for 'he', 'in' for 'at', and a doubled 'many of the'. It fails a verbatim check and must not be the quote source. The first pass said 'a few places'.

The link is http only: https on gdg.org fails with a revoked certificate (CRYPT_E_REVOKED), so tools that upgrade http to https cannot fetch it. Single-host hobby site with an empty <title>, so there is some link-rot risk; prefer the Internet Archive scan.

The entry carries no year or page range. Add 'written 13 July 1863; SHSP 11 (1883): 320-327'. The IA 'date' metadata for vol. 11 says 1876 (series start), not 1883, so date from the title page and page headers instead.

Title naming: the body is 'A Soldier's Account of the Gettysburg Campaign. Letter from George W. Beale (son of General R. L. T. Beale)', while the volume contents list 'Gettysburg Campaign - A Soldier's Letter, by George W. Beale'. These are the same item.

The 9th Virginia Cavalry attribution is not stated in the letter. It is established independently by R. L. T. Beale's 1899 regimental roster (George W. Beale, 1st Lt., Co. C), SHSP vol. 11 ('his four sons' in the Ninth Virginia Cavalry), and the letter's own 9th/13th Virginia references.

The letter is contemporaneous (13 July 1863, ten days after East Cavalry Field) but is a hurried, tired, partly second-hand account, written in rain during the retreat. It exaggerates the Rockville capture (about 200 wagons and 12,000 mules, against Stuart's 125 wagons), reports the Hagerstown and Fortieth Virginia losses by hearsay, and gives no calendar dates (the one date, 'June - -', is blank). Treat as perspective, not fact. The 1883 print also cannot be compared with the 1863 manuscript, so editorial changes by SHSP cannot be ruled out.

Small internal ambiguity: 'Colonel Payne, Captain Billingsly of this regiment ... were captured'. Stuart's report gives Payne as Lieut. Col., 4th Virginia Cavalry (temporarily commanding the 2nd NC). Do not attribute Payne to the 9th Virginia.

rights_basis: The 1863 manuscript is public domain by date. It is an unpublished 1863 document; Harman died long ago and the writer was an unidentified aide. A faithful scan of a 2-D public-domain document adds no new copyright. The host page, however, carries 'Copyright (c) 2020 Archives & Special Collections at Dickinson College. All rights reserved.' The ~75-word transcript and the provenance essay come from the dealer (Catherine Barnes, Historical Autographs), a third party. The essay and Dickinson's item description are copyrighted and must not be quoted. Tier A2 only for the manuscript's own words, read from the image, and only after review. Free to read is not free to reuse.

Description says 'provisions'. Only grain (5,000 bushels, 'Corner Oats') is provisions. The demand is mostly clothing, boots, shoes, hats, sole leather, horse shoes, nails and use of a printing office and two printers.
Authenticity ('not signed by Harman but written and signed on his behalf by an aide') is the dealer's own handwriting research, not an archival finding. It is an assertion by the seller.

Dealer essay says Ewell's corps remained in Carlisle 'until June 29'. Murray's note on the GO 72 broadside (entry 588) says Ewell's troops were leaving on the morning of Tuesday 30 June. Treat departure dates from either as unverified.
Link is insecure http.
Manuscript is a Confederate requisition on a civilian town, not an eyewitness account. It is fine as a primary document but is not 'eyewitness' material.

Harman, chief quartermaster'. The first-pass finding is confirmed: dead link, Wayback only. I differ in that the content is real and verified from the image, and a working replacement exists.
extraction_notes: Use the Wayback PDF. It has a cover sheet and a dealer transcript in the text layer (extractable with pdftotext). PDF pages 2-3 are image-only: the manuscript and the 'Dear Freddy' letter, no OCR. For citation, treat the document as ONE passage (~75 words). Take the words from the manuscript image, not from the dealer essay, and keep the bracketed expansions [Army of Northern Virginia] and [Chief Quarter Master] out of the quote. Provenance facts (dealer sale, sanitary fair letter 20 June 1864) are facts-only. Record the capture timestamp and sha256 in the register because Wayback URLs can change.

written: 1863-06-21 (order dated 'Headquarters Army Northern Va., 21st June, 1863'); the broadside was posted in Carlisle about 27-30 June 1863 (removal on 30 June per the Murray note, as described by Dickinson). Contemporaneous.
rights_basis: The order text is an 1863 Confederate general order, public domain by date, and is also printed in the Official Records, Ser. I, vol. 27 pt 3 p. 912 (US government publication, 1889; entry 1567). For quoting, use the OR text (A1), not this entry. The Dickinson page, scan and description carry 'Copyright (c) 2020 ... All rights reserved'. The Dickinson description and the transcription of Murray's note are third-party text: facts only. The broadside scan itself is a faithful copy of a public-domain printed document, and the preview image is readable only coarsely.
issues: Live link dead: http 301 to https, then 404 (same Drupal 11 'Page not found' as 587). /civil-war-resources also 404.

Title date range 'June 27-30, 1863' is the posting period. It comes from the House Divided finding aid (Wingert 2018) section heading and the Murray removal note, not from the item date. The order is dated 21 June 1863, which is printed on the broadside and listed on the Dickinson page. The start date of 27 June is inferred from Ewell's arrival, not stated on the item page.

Wayback's archived PDF is truncated. Three captures (20191121110548, 20211017064003, 20240812005820) are each exactly 1,048,576 B (a 1 MiB cap), and pdftotext/pymupdf report a damaged file with no xref. extraction_notes: Do not extract text from this host: the Wayback PDF is truncated and the preview image is too small to transcribe reliably. written: 1863-07 (internal evidence: narrative runs to 'July 30th, Battery mustered out of service. Copy of official return on muster roll'); transmitted to Pleasonton in Landis's cover letter of 29 Dec 1863; printed 1864. Contemporaneous within weeks, not a retrospective memoir.
rights_basis: Original 1864 imprint. The OCR title page of the Library of Congress copy (IA reportofbrigadie00phil, leaf n4) reads 'PHILADELPHIA: KING & BAIRD, PRINTERS, No. 607 SANSOM STREET. 1864.' Cornell's catalog record, in a Wayback capture, says Date 1864, Publisher King & Baird. IA metadata for the LoC copy says 'The Library of Congress is unaware of any copyright restrictions for this item' (collections library_of_congress, americana). Published before 1931, so Tier A basis (counsel confirm per the plan). Note that IA's own 'date' field says 1862, which describes the 3-in-1 bound volume; rights must use the title-page year 1864. Use the LoC original-imprint scan, not Cornell's digital collections page, which blocks bots and has its own 'Guidelines for use'.

FIRST-PASS REJECT IS WRONG. 'mayantislavery' is the Samuel J. May Anti-Slavery Pamphlet Collection. It holds this pamphlet (may923305: 'Third annual report of Brigadier General A.J. Pleasonton, commanding the Home guard of the city of Philadelphia, to the Hon. Alexander Henry, mayor for 1863', 114 page images, Philadelphia: King & Baird, 1864). The collection name is misleading, not evidence of a wrong link.

The first pass said no Landis report exists, because the OR has none. Right about the OR, but Landis's report is appended to Pleasonton's pamphlet (his words: 'A copy of Captain Landis' official report of his service ... hereto appended, marked "C."'), where it is the sole primary account by the battery's own captain.

Description is incomplete. This is Landis's whole-service return for 24 June-30 July 1863, as muster-roll return copied into the Third Annual Report. Sporting Hill is one paragraph at the top of printed p. 82, not the whole report. It is embedded in Pleasonton's report as appendix C, a fact the entry omits.

Cornell viewer sequence numbers (seq=90, seq=91) cannot be re-checked because the viewer is gone. By content, printed p. 82 (Sporting Hill, 30 June; Carlisle approach, 1 July) and p. 83 (shelling of Carlisle) match the topics of entries 595 and 599, which fits a seq-to-page offset of 8. This is inference, not seen. Entries 595 and 599 are two pages of the same report and should be merged.

Landis's claim that 'eight or ten rebels were killed and fifteen or twenty wounded' is hearsay ('it was afterwards ascertained'). The OR (Smith No. 407) reports only 4 Union wounded and gives no enemy casualty figure. Printed text also says 'General W. T. Smith, U. S. A.' (error for William F. Smith) and 'about five miles out' where Smith says 4 miles beyond Oyster Point. Landis says a section 'in command of the First Lieutenant' went out; Ewen's report (No. 411) says the section came up 'under command of Lieut. Rufus King, of the army, serving on General W. F. Smith's staff'. Minor differences; quote verbatim and attribute.
Link is insecure http. Cornell offers no free API, and the replacement is a different scan (LoC copy of the same 1864 imprint).

PHILADELPHIA: KING & BAIRD ... 1864.' Pleasonton's text, printed pp. 22-23: Company A, 1st Regiment of Artillery, Capt. H. D. Landis, 116 men, reached Harrisburg the night of 24 June 1863 and was sent to man guns at Fort Washington; 'rendered most important and valuable service, especially at Sporting Hill, and in the defence of Carlisle ... A copy of Captain Landis' official report of his service ... hereto appended, marked "C."' Landis's report begins 'To Brigadier-General A. J. Pleasonton, General: The Battery under my command left Philadelphia June 24th, 1863 ... June 30th, a section in command of the First Lieutenant, was sent out upon the Harrisburg and Carlisle turnpike, to assist General Ewen's brigade, (22d and 37th N. Y. S. V.) which had been attacked by the rebels with artillery and infantry; the brigade was found engaged at Sporting Hill, about five miles out ...' and continues to Carlisle on 1 July ('About 6 1/2 in the evening a rebel force of 3,500 ... commenced an attack upon the town'), the 3 shells fired, the 1-2 July shelling, and march to Hagerstown, signed 'HENRY D. LANDIS, Capt. 1st Philada. Battery'. Mapped by djvu.xml object order: printed p. 82 = leaf n85, p. 83 = n86, p. 85 = n88. I fetched BookReader image https://archive.org/download/reportofbrigadie00phil/page/n85_w900.jpg (234,851 B, sha256 9025b2deea825ae056fdbd00b98ce7819be2b34d0686b6121aa53237e22d126b) and viewed it: it is printed page '82', starting 'To Brigadier-General A. J. Pleasonton, General:—The Battery under my command left Philadelphia June 24th, 1863 ...' with Sporting Hill and the 30 June section. https://archive.org/details/reportofbrigadie00phil returned 200. The sibling item reportofbrigadie00phil_0 (State Library of PA, 30 images) contains only the 1861 report. CROSS-CHECKS against the OR vol. 27 pt 2 cache: Smith's report No. 407 (Greencastle, 18 July 1863): 'A reconnaissance was made on the 30th ... by Colonel Brisbane, with one section of Landis' battery, to Sporting Hill, 4 miles beyond Oyster Point, which resulted in a skirmish, in which we had 4 wounded' and 'Wednesday, July 1. The brigades of General Ewen and Colonel Brisbane, with Landis' battery, moved to Carlisle'. Ewen's report No. 411: 'a section of a battery, called Landis' battery, belonging to a company of gentlemen from Philadelphia, came up, under command of Lieut. Rufus King ... I immediately posted one piece in the road, and the other in rear of a dwelling'. The OR index sends Sporting Hill to 'Reports of Smith, p. 223; [Ewen], p. 233'. Landis himself has no OR report. CLAIM CHECKS: (1) Union militia battery: Philadelphia Home Guard, Co. A, 1st Reg. Artillery, mustered into US service 24 June 1863, confirmed. (2) Sporting Hill engagement, 30 June: confirmed independently by Smith and Ewen.
extraction_notes: Source for ingestion: IA reportofbrigadie00phil, _djvu.txt (224 KB) has NO form feeds, so segment with _djvu.xml (2.5 MB, 120 OBJECT leaves, 0-based). For the Third Annual Report pages 22-86, leaf index = printed page + 3 (p. 22 = n25, p. 82 = n85, p. 83 = n86, p. 85 = n88, p. 86 = n89). Cite as 'Third Annual Report of Brig. Gen. A. J. Pleasonton ... Home Guard of the City of Philadelphia (Philadelphia: King & Baird, 1864), App. C, p. 82', via archive.org, with View scan. The report covers printed pp. 82-85 (ends before the 'Extract from the Report of Captain Thomas B. Dwight', pp. 86-92, n89-n95, a second eyewitness narrative of the same actions by an aide-de-camp, which is a further passage worth adding). OCR is fair-good. Seen errors: 'Avhole' (whole), 'withdraAvn', 'Kewman's Cut' (Newman's Cut), 'tlie', '6J', 'Sporting Plill', stray carets. All are caught by the corpus verbatim check against the image. The page image is clean. The printed 'W. T. Smith' error must be kept in quotes and linked to W. F. Smith. Whole-service text, so one report of about 4 pages. Pleasonton's own prose around it is a separate Union staff voice. Mark contemporaneous and Union militia.
